text:
The "Chinese room" thought experiment, proposed by philosopher John Searle in 1980, challenges the validity of the Strong AI hypothesis, which posits that a properly programmed computer possesses a mind in the same sense as a human. Searle argues that a person who understands only English but follows a rulebook to manipulate Chinese symbols (the "Chinese room") can produce perfect Chinese responses without actually understanding the meaning of the characters. He concludes that because the process relies solely on syntactic symbol manipulation without semantic understanding (intentionality), the system lacks a mind or consciousness. Searle identifies this as a fundamental flaw in functionalism and computationalism, asserting that syntax alone is insufficient to generate semantics, and that specific biological machinery in the brain is necessary for mental phenomena.
The argument has sparked extensive debate, leading to various counter-arguments such as the "system reply," which suggests the entire setup (person plus rules and tools) constitutes the understanding, or the "robot reply," which proposes that connecting the system to the physical world via sensors could ground the symbols in meaning. Critics like Stevan Harnad and David Chalmers defend the computational theory of mind, arguing that the Turing test is a valid operational measure of intelligence regardless of internal mechanisms, or that large language models demonstrate robust internal representations. Conversely, Searle maintains that no matter how complex the program or how it is connected to the world, if the components do not possess understanding, the system as a whole does not either, effectively proving that computers running programs cannot think in the human sense.
